title: A general experimental reading of viral genes that have no recognizable relatives

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a general method for discovering what viral proteins do when their sequences have no recognizable relationship to proteins with established functions. It would connect an unfamiliar viral gene to a specific molecular activity and establish how that activity affects the host during infection. Computational predictions could guide the experiments, but a predicted structure or an inherited annotation would not by itself establish the function.

The intended advance is repeatable experimental interpretation across many unfamiliar protein families, extending beyond isolated discoveries in a few tractable viruses. This requires distinguishing several kinds of uncertainty: a protein can have recognizable relatives whose functions are also unknown, lack detectable sequence relatives yet have an informative predicted structure, or remain functionally obscure despite both sequence and structural analysis. Lack of an annotation and lack of homology are therefore different problems, although both contribute to viral dark matter.

significance.text: A broadly validated method would make substantial, currently obscure portions of sampled viral genomes functionally interpretable. It would turn lists of hypothetical proteins into testable mechanisms of infection and host manipulation, expanding functional virology beyond genes already connected to characterized proteins. The direct benefit would be a stronger mechanistic interpretation of metagenomes, virus–host interactions and auxiliary viral genes within the method’s demonstrated coverage.

Some auxiliary viral genes affect or are predicted to affect carbon, nitrogen and other microbial metabolic processes. Resolving their activities could explain how infection changes host metabolism and help identify previously unknown enzymes or regulatory mechanisms. Extending these findings to ecosystem-wide nutrient flows would require ecological measurements of abundance, expression, host context and environmental effects. Discovering a protein’s activity does not establish the magnitude of its influence in nature.

Useful enzymes, antiviral targets and improved phage therapies are conditional downstream possibilities. Each would still require application-specific development and validation; a general functional interpretation method would supply mechanisms and candidates rather than finished medicines or reliable therapeutic performance.

Synthesis: making viral genomes functionally readable would not amount to a planetary census. Cataloging viral diversity requires representative sampling and sequencing, while counting individual particles is a separate observation problem. Functional interpretation could improve understanding of collected samples without identifying every viral lineage or enumerating every particle on Earth. The approximately 10^31 particle estimate mentioned in the earlier research is not established by the supplied evidence and is unnecessary to the significance of this innovation.

missing_breakthrough.text: The missing capability is a scalable experimental connection from an unfamiliar viral protein to a validated molecular function and an infection-relevant host effect. Rapid viral sequence evolution limits the reach of sequence-based annotation. Structural inference and genome neighborhood can suggest plausible functions, but those suggestions still need experiments that distinguish the proposed mechanism from alternative explanations.

Experimental access is a separate barrier. Many relevant hosts cannot readily be cultured, and a protein’s activity may depend on its host, interaction partners or infection context. An activity observed in an isolated biochemical assay may not explain what the protein does during infection. Conversely, an altered host phenotype does not on its own identify the molecular mechanism. The review discusses complementary approaches such as biochemical assays, complementation, viral gene deletion and host-physiology measurements, whose integration remains difficult at the scale of newly discovered genes.

Breadth adds another engineering challenge: a common discovery workflow must accommodate diverse activities and experimental systems without reducing every protein to the same assay. A requirement for a biochemical activity deliberately narrows the benchmark for proteins whose principal roles are structural or depend on molecular interactions. A credible general method must either declare those boundaries or provide appropriate ways to test such roles, rather than treating an unsuitable assay as evidence that a protein has no function.

current_state.text: Kosmopoulos and Anantharaman’s review, Viral Dark Matter: Illuminating Protein Function, Ecology, and Biotechnological Promises, published on 20 November 2025, reports that 40–90% of viral genes across surveyed environments lack known homologues or annotated functions. It also reports that roughly 40–45% of proteins and 75–85% of protein families in the reference databases discussed are hypothetical or unknown. These figures use different datasets and denominators; they do not establish that every unannotated protein lacks homologues. The surveyed evidence also has substantial sampling bias toward double-stranded DNA viruses.

The same review reports more than 15 million viral sequences in IMG/VR v4 and more than 450,000 protein clusters in a gut-virome catalog, with 92% of those clusters previously undocumented. These are measures of accumulated sequence discovery and catalog novelty, not counts of experimentally established functions. Together with the review’s discussion of experimental capacity, they illustrate why sequence discovery is outpacing functional characterization.

There is real experimental progress in individual systems: the review describes characterized auxiliary metabolic and regulatory viral genes, alongside computational methods that use predicted structures and genomic context to nominate functions. Some phage-gene activities have been experimentally validated, while many other proposed activities remain untested. These achievements establish useful components and case studies, but the supplied sources do not demonstrate the proposed broad method across unfamiliar viral protein families.

Lu and colleagues’ mSphere analysis, Estimated size of the total genome and protein space of viruses, published on 25 February 2025, estimates that less than 3% of viral genetic diversity had been uncovered. More specifically, its estimates imply coverage of 0.94% of viral operational taxonomic units and 2.50% of protein clusters. These are model-dependent extrapolations from IMG/VR, using an operational saturation assumption under which fewer than one novel virus would be identified in a sample. They measure estimated coverage of genetic diversity, not the fraction of viral proteins with known functions or a direct census of individual viruses. Ecosystem, geographic and RNA-virus sampling biases limit interpretation.

The supplied review could assess the relevant body text of the Kosmopoulos–Anantharaman article, although its retained extraction was truncated in the references and its figures were not inspected. Its numerical summaries are therefore supported as reported by that review, without independent verification of plotted values. For the mSphere study, the supplied review assessed a complete main-article XML extraction, but not linked supplements or figure images. These access limits do not negate the dated findings, but they bound the verification represented here.

The research also attributes a statement about incomplete geographic coverage of species’ viromes to Holmes, Krammer and Goodrum’s September 2024 Cell article. No retained artifact for that source was supplied, so the specific assertion cannot be verified from this record. Separately, the supplied freshness search record is empty: the dated publications do not establish whether a broadly validated method had become available by 1 November 2026. The supplied evidence therefore leaves present availability unresolved rather than proving that no such method exists.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: conduct a blinded evaluation on a pre-set panel on the order of hundreds of viral protein families lacking detectable sequence homology to characterized proteins, including both phages and eukaryotic viruses. Before testing, define the homology search procedure, reference databases, panel composition, success threshold and treatment of uncertain results. Panel selection should make the claimed coverage assessable and prevent success in a few experimentally convenient groups from standing in for broad performance.
completion_criteria.label: Blinded evaluation covers hundreds of families lacking characterized homologs

completion_criteria.text: Proposed functional requirement: predict a specific biochemical activity and a host-level effect, then confirm both with appropriate experiments for a large, pre-specified share of the panel. Assay controls should distinguish the proposed activity from nonspecific effects, and host-context experiments should test whether it explains the relevant infection phenotype. Depending on the system, evidence could combine biochemical measurements with complementation, viral gene deletion and host physiology. Structure prediction and annotation transfer would be useful inputs, but would not satisfy experimental confirmation by themselves.
completion_criteria.label: Experiments confirm activities and host effects across large pre-specified shares

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility requirement: independent laboratories should reproduce representative molecular and host-context findings using disclosed protocols, and the workflow should retain useful performance on additional families not used to develop it. Results should report failures and uncertainty, including coverage differences between viral groups and the practical burden of obtaining suitable hosts and assays. The treatment of structural and interaction-dependent proteins must be explicit so that the demonstrated scope is clear.
completion_criteria.label: Independent laboratories reproduce findings; workflow retains performance on additional families

completion_criteria.text: The panel size, performance threshold and replication requirements above are proposals, not established community standards. A finite test would demonstrate breadth across its sampled families and conditions, not literal universality. A complete planetary viral catalog is unnecessary, and successful functional interpretation would not by itself establish ecosystem effects or therapeutic utility.
completion_criteria.label: Reported scope limits claims to sampled viral families and conditions

related_concepts.text: Synthesis from the supplied roster: VIR-01, A prospective sequence-to-phenotype theory of infectivity, transmission, and escape, overlaps through the need to connect viral sequence with mechanism. VIR-08 focuses on experimentally resolving unfamiliar proteins; VIR-01 seeks prospective predictions of higher-level viral phenotypes. Characterizing a protein could supply mechanistic inputs to VIR-01, but does not alone predict infectivity, transmission or escape.

Synthesis from the supplied roster: VIR-02, Empiric medicines that cover the major causes of severe acute viral disease, and VIR-03, Scalable elimination or permanent silencing of persistent viral genomes, could benefit from newly identified viral mechanisms or targets. VIR-11, An interruptible causal chain from a persistent virus to a major chronic disease, could likewise use experimentally characterized proteins in causal studies. These concepts separately require evidence of treatment coverage, durable control of persistent genomes, or disease causation and interruption; protein-function discovery does not establish those outcomes.

Synthesis from the supplied roster: VIR-04, Protective immunity that covers a viral family, including future variants and unseen relatives; VIR-05, Durable immunity at the respiratory surface that stops transmission; and VIR-09, A mechanistic correlate that predicts human protection from a new virus, all overlap with functional virology and host interactions. VIR-08 could reveal relevant immune-modulating proteins, but its biochemical and host-level validation would not establish broad immune coverage, durable respiratory protection or a predictive human correlate.

Synthesis from the supplied roster: VIR-06, Bacteriophage therapy that can be prescribed as reliably as an antibacterial drug, has a particularly direct connection because resolving unfamiliar phage genes could improve understanding of phage–host interactions. Reliable prescribing additionally requires therapeutic performance and clinical predictability. Functional annotation is an enabling capability rather than a substitute for those demonstrations.

Synthesis from the supplied roster: VIR-07, Viral particles that can be aimed at chosen human cells, given again, and carry large genes, and VIR-10, A single-dose, conditionally replicating interfering particle that keeps a chronic virus suppressed, concern engineered delivery or intervention systems. Discovering unfamiliar viral protein functions could inform their design, but targeting, repeat dosing, cargo capacity, conditional replication and sustained suppression require distinct engineering and validation. VIR-08 remains the discovery capability shared with these applications, rather than a merger of their objectives.

change_log.change: Preserved VIR-08’s identity and integrated the research’s explanatory detail with the review’s distinctions between sequence novelty, missing annotation and experimental uncertainty.
change_log.reason: These are related but different scientific problems, and the original wording sometimes treated them as interchangeable.

change_log.change: Separated rapid sequence evolution as a limitation on homology-based inference from uncultivated hosts and contextual activity as barriers to experimental validation.
change_log.reason: Host culturability does not directly determine whether sequence homology can be detected.

change_log.change: Retained the reported percentages, sequence totals and protein-cluster figures with their dataset scope and dsDNA sampling bias.
change_log.reason: The supplied review supports these summaries, but their denominators differ and catalog novelty does not establish functional novelty.

change_log.change: Expanded the mSphere estimate with 0.94% vOTU coverage, 2.50% protein-cluster coverage, operational saturation assumptions and sampling limitations.
change_log.reason: The less-than-3% estimate concerns extrapolated genetic diversity rather than functional understanding or particle counts.

change_log.change: Removed the claimed inference from functional interpretation and sampling to a literal planetary particle census, while preserving the distinction and qualifying the approximately 10^31 estimate.
change_log.reason: Neither the count nor that causal inference is established by the supplied evidence; neither is necessary to preserve the innovation.

change_log.change: Restricted direct impact claims to experimentally demonstrated functional coverage and separated ecological and therapeutic possibilities.
change_log.reason: Ecosystem effects and applications require additional contextual measurements and development.

change_log.change: Made the proposed benchmark operational through pre-specified searches, panel composition, thresholds, controls, uncertainty reporting and independent replication.
change_log.reason: Hundreds of families alone cannot establish generality, and proposed criteria must remain distinct from published standards.

change_log.change: Preserved the benchmark’s limitation for structural and interaction-dependent proteins.
change_log.reason: Requiring a biochemical activity narrows coverage unless appropriate functional assays are explicitly included.

change_log.change: Qualified the Cell geographic-coverage assertion and the conclusion about present availability, and retained extraction and inspection limitations.
change_log.reason: The Cell artifact was absent, the freshness record was empty, and the supplied review did not inspect every figure or supplement.

change_log.change: Explained overlap and distinctions with every other supplied roster entry without merging concepts.
change_log.reason: A functional discovery capability may enable several applications while remaining distinct from their required outcomes.

unresolved_issues: Whether a method meeting this broad experimental scope was available by 1 November 2026 remains unresolved because no bounded freshness search record was supplied.
The geographic-coverage assertion attributed to Holmes, Krammer and Goodrum cannot be verified without a retained source artifact.
The benchmark still requires a chosen success fraction, exact homology detection procedure, detailed panel composition and assay-specific acceptance criteria.
The scope of biochemical activity requirements for proteins with primarily structural or interaction-dependent roles remains to be defined.
The supplied evidence does not establish the approximately 10^31 viral-particle estimate; it is unnecessary to the concept’s proposed demonstration.

Figures in the 2025 functional review and figures and supplementary material in the mSphere study were not inspected in the supplied review, limiting independent verification beyond the retained prose.

brief.title: Finding out what unfamiliar viral genes do
possible: Scientists could take a viral gene with no recognizable relatives whose jobs are known and work out what its protein does. Experiments would connect that molecular activity to its effect on the host, the organism the virus infects.

They could do this repeatedly across many unfamiliar protein families, groups of related proteins. That would turn growing lists of unknown genes into explanations of how viruses infect and alter their hosts.
why: Researchers studying viruses in environmental samples would gain a clearer understanding of how infection changes microbes. They could explain how particular viral genes alter the chemical processes that keep host cells running.
Identifying these activities could also reveal useful enzymes, proteins that carry out chemical reactions, and candidates for antiviral treatments or therapies using viruses that infect bacteria.

sources.showed: This article discusses incomplete geographic coverage of the viruses associated with host species.
sources.cited_for: It supports the concern that geographic sampling leaves gaps in knowledge of viral diversity.
sources.not_established: Geographic coverage does not establish what unfamiliar viral proteins do.

sources.who: James C Kosmopoulos and Karthik Anantharaman
sources.showed: Their review brings together examples of experimentally characterized viral genes and methods for proposing functions. It describes a widening gap between discovering genes and understanding their activities.
sources.quote:
The gap between viral gene discovery and functional characterization
is widening: modern metagenomic studies are uncovering millions of
new viral genes and genomes, yet most of these encode proteins of
unknown function.
sources.cited_for: It supports the need to connect predicted functions with experiments on molecular activity and effects during infection.
sources.not_established: Individual examples do not establish a repeatable method that works across many unfamiliar protein families.

sources.showed: Their model estimates that less than 3% of viral genetic diversity has been discovered. It extrapolates from the growth of diversity found in sequenced samples.
sources.quote: Remarkably, less than 3% of this large diversity has been uncovered to date.
sources.cited_for: It supports the scale of unexplored viral genetic diversity.
sources.not_established: The estimate depends on modeling assumptions and sampling biases; it does not measure how many viral proteins have known functions.

shown: Researchers have established the activities of some viral genes in individual systems. Kosmopoulos and Anantharaman describe examples that affect host metabolism and gene regulation, alongside computational methods that suggest further functions.

These successes provide parts of a broader approach. They have not demonstrated a general experimental method across many unfamiliar protein families. A predicted protein shape alone does not establish what the protein does during infection.
missing: A repeatable method must connect unfamiliar proteins to both specific molecular activities and effects during infection.
Experiments must distinguish a proposed mechanism from nonspecific effects and competing explanations.
The method must work across diverse viral families, including systems whose hosts are difficult to grow in the laboratory.
Suitable tests must cover proteins that build structures or work through molecular interactions, or explicitly define their exclusion.

milestones.label: A blinded test spans hundreds of unfamiliar protein families
milestones.explanation: A blinded evaluation would have to use a predefined panel spanning viruses of bacteria and more complex organisms, with clear rules for detecting known relatives. This would establish the breadth being tested.

milestones.label: Experiments confirm molecular activities and host effects
milestones.explanation: Controlled experiments would have to confirm predicted activities and explain infection effects for a large, predefined share of the panel. This would connect proposed functions to what proteins actually do.

milestones.label: Other laboratories reproduce results and new families remain tractable
milestones.explanation: Independent laboratories would have to reproduce representative findings, and the method would have to retain useful performance on additional families. This would test whether success extends beyond its developers and original examples.

milestones.label: Claims stay within the tested families and conditions
milestones.explanation: Results would have to state their tested scope and limits. This would establish broad usefulness without implying universal coverage, ecosystem effects or therapeutic success.

uncertain: The required success rate, panel composition and rules for detecting known relatives remain to be defined.
It remains unclear how to judge proteins whose main roles involve building structures or interacting with other molecules.
A protein's activity may depend on its host and infection conditions, complicating how broadly a successful result applies.
